title: Microeconomics of insurance
text:
Before studying the demand for insurance, we need a language for comparing risky situations. We shall use the expected-utility framework associated with von Neumann and Morgenstern. The point is not that individuals literally write down a utility function before making a decision; rather, the model gives a coherent mathematical representation of preferences under risk and a convenient language in which to study risk aversion.


Fix a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\). In this section, random variables represent wealth; later, when we focus on insurance, random variables will often represent losses. Let \(\mathcal I\subseteq\mathbb R\) be an interval, typically \(\mathbb R\), \(\mathbb R_+=[0,\infty)\) or \(\mathbb R_+^*=(0,\infty)\).
We assume that an agent’s preferences over random wealth levels taking values in \(\mathcal I\) admit an expected-utility representation: there exists a function \(u:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[
X \precsim_u Y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb E[u(X)]\leq \mathbb E[u(Y)].
\]
Here \(X\precsim_u Y\) means that the agent weakly prefers \(Y\) to \(X\). Equality defines indifference:
\[
X\sim_u Y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb E[u(X)]=\mathbb E[u(Y)].
\]
Throughout this chapter, we restrict attention to random variables for which all the expectations under consideration are well defined and finite. The precise integrability conditions depend jointly on the random variable and on the utility function, and will not be repeated each time.






NoteUtility is not unique



If \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), then \(u\) and
\[
\widetilde u=\alpha u+\beta
\]
represent exactly the same preferences. Any economically meaningful quantity derived from utility should therefore be invariant under positive affine transformations.


We shall assume throughout that \(u\) is continuous on its domain and twice continuously differentiable on the interior of its domain, with
\[
u'(x)>0,
\qquad
u''(x)\leq 0.
\]
The first condition says that more wealth is preferred to less. The second says that the marginal utility of wealth is non-increasing: an additional euro matters less when wealth is already high. The condition \(u''<0\) on the interior of \(\mathcal I\) is a convenient sufficient condition for strict risk aversion; if \(u''(x)=0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\), then \(u\) is affine and increasing (we often normalise it to \(u(x)=x\)), and the agent is risk-neutral.
The geometry of concavity is useful to keep in mind. For \(x_0,x_1\in\mathcal I\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
u\bigl(\theta x_0+(1-\theta)x_1\bigr)
\geq
\theta u(x_0)+(1-\theta)u(x_1).
\]
The graph of a concave utility function therefore lies above every chord joining two points of the graph.








Figure 1: The utility of an average wealth lies above the corresponding average utility because of concavity.





Concavity has an immediate interpretation under uncertainty.

Theorem 1 (Jensen’s inequality) Let \(u\) be concave and let \(X\) be an integrable random variable such that \(u(X)\) is integrable. Then
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u\bigl(\mathbb E[X]\bigr).
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, meaning that \(X\) is not almost surely constant, the inequality is strict.

Since \(u\) is increasing, Jensen’s inequality means that a risk-averse agent weakly prefers the sure amount \(\mathbb E[X]\) to the random wealth \(X\):
\[
X\precsim_u \mathbb E[X].
\]
A simple classroom example makes the point. Consider the choice between a sure €1 and a fair coin toss paying €0 or €2. At such small stakes, many people are close to indifferent. Multiply all amounts by 10,000 and the reaction is usually quite different: the sure €10,000 is overwhelmingly preferred to a fair gamble between €0 and €20,000. At still larger stakes the effect becomes even clearer. Faced, for instance, with a sure €250,000 rather than a fair gamble between €0 and €1,000,000, virtually everyone in a typical classroom chooses the sure amount, even though it is only half the expected payoff of the gamble.



The previous example suggests a natural way of attaching a monetary value to a risky prospect.

Definition 1 (Certainty equivalent) Let \(X\) take values in \(\mathcal I\) and assume that \(u(X)\) is integrable. The certainty equivalent of \(X\) for utility \(u\) is the unique sure wealth level \(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\in\mathcal I\) satisfying
\[
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr)
=
\mathbb E[u(X)].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(X)]\right).
\]
In French, the same object is the équivalent certain, often denoted \(ec_u(X)\).

The certainty equivalent is a monetary valuation of final wealth: it is the sure wealth level that makes the agent indifferent to the risky wealth \(X\).






NoteCertainty equivalents and indifference prices



When the random variable represents an incremental payoff rather than final wealth, it is often more natural to speak of an indifference price.
Suppose an agent has initial wealth \(w\) and considers buying a risky payoff \(Y\) for a price \(p\). The buyer’s indifference price \(p_u(w,Y)\) is defined, when it exists, by
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[u\bigl(w+Y-p_u(w,Y)\bigr)\right]
=
u(w).
\]
It is the maximum price that leaves the agent indifferent between buying the gamble and keeping the initial wealth for certain. In general, this price depends on the background wealth \(w\). It should therefore not be confused with \(\operatorname{ce}_u(Y)\). Under CARA utility (see below) on \(\mathbb R\), however, translation invariance removes the wealth effect and one obtains exactly
\[
p_u(w,Y)=\operatorname{ce}_u(Y).
\]



Proposition 1 (Certainty equivalent and the mean) Let \(u\) be increasing and concave. Whenever the quantities are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, the inequality is strict.


Proof. By Jensen’s inequality,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u(\mathbb E[X]).
\]
By definition,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is strictly increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
Strict concavity and non-degeneracy give the strict version through the strict form of Jensen’s inequality.

The difference
\[
\pi_u(X)
:=
\mathbb E[X]-\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\geq0
\]
is called the risk premium. It is the discount, relative to mean wealth, associated with bearing the risk.






NoteThe St Petersburg paradox



The St Petersburg paradox is an early illustration of why expected monetary value is not enough to describe choices under risk. Nicolas Bernoulli posed the problem in correspondence in 1713. A fair coin is tossed until the first head appears; if this occurs on toss \(n\), the payoff is \(2^n\). The expected monetary payoff is infinite, since every possible stopping time contributes the same positive amount to the expectation. Yet the fact that the expected payoff is infinite does not make an arbitrarily large entry fee attractive.
Daniel Bernoulli’s celebrated 1738 response was to value wealth through a concave utility function rather than to maximise expected money directly. His central example was logarithmic utility. The episode is historically important because it makes the distinction between money and the utility of money explicit, long before the axiomatic formulation of expected utility by von Neumann and Morgenstern. See Bernoulli (1738/1954).





The certainty equivalent depends both on the distribution of the risk and on the agent’s utility function. For a small risk, these two effects separate particularly cleanly.
Let
\[
X_\varepsilon=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\]
where
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Thus \(\mu\) is the mean wealth and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2.
\]

Proposition 2 (Certainty equivalent of a small centred risk) Let \(\mu\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal I\). Assume that \(u\) is twice continuously differentiable in a neighbourhood of \(\mu\), with \(u'(\mu)>0\), and that \(Z\) is bounded with
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Then, as \(\varepsilon\to0\),
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac12\frac{u''(\mu)}{u'(\mu)}\,\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]


Proof. A second-order Taylor expansion of \(u\) at \(\mu\) gives
\[
u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u(\mu)
+
u'(\mu)\varepsilon Z
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2Z^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
where boundedness of \(Z\) makes the remainder uniform for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\). Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[Z^2]=1\),
\[
\mathbb E[u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)]
=
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right).
\]
Since \(u'(\mu)>0\), the inverse function theorem gives
\[
\bigl(u^{-1}\bigr)'(u(\mu))
=
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}.
\]
A first-order expansion of \(u^{-1}\) at \(u(\mu)\) therefore yields
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}
\left(
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right),
\]
which is the stated result.

The expansion separates two ingredients. The amount of risk is represented by the variance \(\varepsilon^2\), while the local attitude towards risk is captured by the curvature ratio evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).
This motivates the fundamental definition.

Definition 2 (Risk aversion coefficients) The coefficient of absolute risk aversion is
\[
\gamma_u(x)
:=
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}.
\]
For \(x>0\), the corresponding coefficient of relative risk aversion is
\[
\rho_u(x)
:=
x\,\gamma_u(x).
\]

The coefficient is classically associated with the work of Arrow and Pratt (1964).
Because \(u\) is concave and increasing, \(\gamma_u(x)\geq0\). More importantly, \(\gamma_u\) is unchanged when \(u\) is replaced by \(\alpha u+\beta\) with \(\alpha>0\): it therefore depends on preferences, not on the arbitrary choice of a utility representation.
With this notation, Proposition 2 becomes
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
-
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
\pi_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
The leading-order cost of a small risk is therefore the product of a risk term, its variance, and a preference term, the coefficient of absolute risk aversion evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).



A particularly tractable case is constant absolute risk aversion (CARA).

Proposition 3 (Characterisation of CARA utility) Suppose \(u'>0\) and
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\gamma
\]
for every \(x\) in an interval, where \(\gamma\geq0\) is constant. Then:

if \(\gamma=0\), \(u\) is affine and the agent is risk-neutral;
if \(\gamma>0\), then, up to a positive affine transformation,

\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}.
\]
Conversely, \(u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}\) has constant absolute risk aversion equal to \(\gamma\).


Proof. The equation \(\gamma_u(x)=\gamma\) is
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\gamma,
\]
or equivalently
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\gamma.
\]
Hence
\[
u'(x)
=
C e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad C>0.
\]
If \(\gamma>0\), integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A-B e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad B>0,
\]
which is equivalent under a positive affine transformation to \(-e^{-\gamma x}\). If \(\gamma=0\), then \(u'\) is constant and \(u\) is affine.

CARA is a strong assumption for individuals because willingness to bear a fixed monetary risk does not depend on wealth. It is nevertheless extremely convenient. In particular, for
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad \gamma>0,
\]
we have
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
-\frac1\gamma
\log\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma X}],
\]
whenever the expectation is finite, and
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X+c)
=
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)+c.
\]
This translation invariance is one reason CARA specifications are common in models of firms or delegated decision-makers when one wants to analyse profit risk without modelling wealth effects explicitly.
For Gaussian risks the small-risk approximation is not an approximation at all.

Proposition 4 (CARA utility and Gaussian wealth) Let
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad \gamma>0,
\]
and let
\[
X=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\varepsilon^2.
\]

The calculation uses the Laplace transform of a standard Gaussian, or equivalently its moment-generating function:
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]

Proof. Since
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2},
\]
we obtain
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
-e^{-\gamma\mu}
\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma\varepsilon Z}]
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\varepsilon^2
\right).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
-e^{-\gamma\operatorname{ce}_u(X)}
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\varepsilon^2
\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\varepsilon^2.
\]
Since \(\gamma_u\equiv\gamma\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\varepsilon^2\), the above second-order formula is exact in this Gaussian/CARA case.







NoteTwo proofs of the Gaussian Laplace transform





Let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and define
\[
M(t)
=
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}].
\]
We show that
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]
1. Completing the square. Using the Gaussian density,
\[
M(t)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
\exp\!\left(
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,dz.
\]
Since
\[
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
=
-\frac{(z-t)^2}{2}
+
\frac{t^2}{2},
\]
we obtain
\[
M(t)
=
e^{t^2/2}
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
e^{-(z-t)^2/2}\,dz
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]
2. A differential equation. Differentiating under the expectation,
\[
M'(t)
=
\mathbb E[Ze^{tZ}].
\]
Gaussian integration by parts gives
\[
\mathbb E[Zf(Z)]
=
\mathbb E[f'(Z)].
\]
With \(f(z)=e^{tz}\),
\[
M'(t)
=
tM(t).
\]
Together with \(M(0)=1\), this differential equation has the unique solution
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]






Absolute risk aversion need not be constant. We say that utility has

DARA (decreasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u'(x)<0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\);
IARA (increasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u'(x)>0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\).

For individual decision-making, DARA is often regarded as more plausible than CARA: as wealth increases, a fixed monetary gamble becomes less important relative to the agent’s resources. Some empirical work finds absolute risk aversion decreasing with wealth, but the evidence is not uniform and estimated risk attitudes vary substantially across people and elicitation methods. DARA is therefore best viewed as an economically useful benchmark rather than as a universal empirical law; see, for example, Guiso and Paiella (2008) and the rather different insurance-choice evidence in Cohen and Einav (2007).
A second classical family imposes constant relative rather than absolute risk aversion.

Proposition 5 (Characterisation of CRRA utility) Let the domain be \((0,\infty)\) and suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\qquad
\rho>0.
\]
Then, up to a positive affine transformation,
\[
u(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho},
& \rho\neq1,\\[1.1ex]
\log x,
& \rho=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Conversely, these utility functions satisfy
\[
\rho_u(x)
=
x\gamma_u(x)
=
\rho,
\]
and therefore have constant relative risk aversion.


Proof. The equation
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
gives
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\]
hence
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\frac{\rho}{x}.
\]
Integrating,
\[
u'(x)
=
C x^{-\rho},
\qquad C>0.
\]
A second integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\frac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}
\]
when \(\rho\neq1\), and
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\log x
\]
when \(\rho=1\), with \(B>0\). Positive affine transformations remove the irrelevant constants.

CRRA utility is DARA because
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
decreases with wealth. It also imposes a very specific rate of decline: doubling wealth halves absolute risk aversion. This restriction is often too rigid empirically. The logarithmic case \(\rho=1\) is the specification associated with Daniel Bernoulli’s classical discussion of the St Petersburg paradox.



People can often answer questions about certainty equivalents – what sure amount would make you indifferent to this lottery? – much more readily than they can specify or draw an entire utility function. It is therefore useful to have a way of comparing the risk aversion of two agents without assigning cardinal meaning to the vertical scales of their utility functions.
Consider one agent represented by utility \(u\) and another represented by utility \(v\). The key mathematical idea is concavification: one agent is more risk-averse than the other precisely when their utility can be obtained from the other’s by applying an additional increasing concave transformation.

Proposition 6 (Comparison of risk aversion) Let \(u\) and \(v\) be twice continuously differentiable, strictly increasing utility functions on the same interval \(\mathcal I\). Then the following statements are equivalent:

for every \(x\in\mathcal I\),
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x);
\]
there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) on \(v(\mathcal I)\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]


In words, the agent represented by \(u\) is more risk-averse than the agent represented by \(v\) exactly when \(u\) is an increasing concave transformation of \(v\).

Proof. Because \(v\) is strictly increasing, it is invertible on its range. Define
\[
g
:=
u\circ v^{-1}.
\]
Then \(u=g\circ v\), and \(g\) is increasing because both \(u\) and \(v^{-1}\) are increasing. Differentiating the identity
\[
g(v(x))
=
u(x)
\]
gives
\[
g'(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{v'(x)}
>
0.
\]
Differentiating once more,
\[
g''(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\left(
\gamma_v(x)-\gamma_u(x)
\right).
\]
The factor
\[
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\]
is positive. Hence
\[
g''\leq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gamma_u\geq\gamma_v.
\]
This proves both directions.

The comparison has an immediate implication for certainty equivalents.

Proposition 7 (Ordering of certainty equivalents) Suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x)
\]
for every \(x\in\mathcal I\). Then, for every random variable \(X\) for which the certainty equivalents are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]

Thus, when the agent represented by \(u\) is more risk-averse than the agent represented by \(v\), they assign a lower certainty equivalent to every risky prospect.

Proof. By Proposition 6, there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
\mathbb E[g(v(X))]
\leq
g\bigl(\mathbb E[v(X)]\bigr).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent under \(v\),
\[
\mathbb E[v(X)]
=
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
g\!\left(
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr)
\right)
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
But
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]

\mathbb E[X].
\]
Strict concavity and non-degeneracy give the strict version through the strict form of Jensen’s inequality.

The difference
\[
\pi_u(X)
:=
\mathbb E[X]-\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\geq0
\]
is called the risk premium. It is the discount, relative to mean wealth, associated with bearing the risk.






NoteThe St Petersburg paradox



The St Petersburg paradox is an early illustration of why expected monetary value is not enough to describe choices under risk. Nicolas Bernoulli posed the problem in correspondence in 1713. A fair coin is tossed until the first head appears; if this occurs on toss \(n\), the payoff is \(2^n\). The expected monetary payoff is infinite, since every possible stopping time contributes the same positive amount to the expectation. Yet the fact that the expected payoff is infinite does not make an arbitrarily large entry fee attractive.
Daniel Bernoulli’s celebrated 1738 response was to value wealth through a concave utility function rather than to maximise expected money directly. His central example was logarithmic utility. The episode is historically important because it makes the distinction between money and the utility of money explicit, long before the axiomatic formulation of expected utility by von Neumann and Morgenstern. See Bernoulli (1738/1954).





The certainty equivalent depends both on the distribution of the risk and on the agent’s utility function. For a small risk, these two effects separate particularly cleanly.
Let
\[
X_\varepsilon=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\]
where
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Thus \(\mu\) is the mean wealth and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2.
\]

Proposition 2 (Certainty equivalent of a small centred risk) Let \(\mu\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal I\). Assume that \(u\) is twice continuously differentiable in a neighbourhood of \(\mu\), with \(u'(\mu)>0\), and that \(Z\) is bounded with
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Then, as \(\varepsilon\to0\),
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac12\frac{u''(\mu)}{u'(\mu)}\,\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]


Proof. A second-order Taylor expansion of \(u\) at \(\mu\) gives
\[
u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u(\mu)
+
u'(\mu)\varepsilon Z
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2Z^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
where boundedness of \(Z\) makes the remainder uniform for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\). Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[Z^2]=1\),
\[
\mathbb E[u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)]
=
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right).
\]
Since \(u'(\mu)>0\), the inverse function theorem gives
\[
\bigl(u^{-1}\bigr)'(u(\mu))
=
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}.
\]
A first-order expansion of \(u^{-1}\) at \(u(\mu)\) therefore yields
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}
\left(
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right),
\]
which is the stated result.

The expansion separates two ingredients. The amount of risk is represented by the variance \(\varepsilon^2\), while the local attitude towards risk is captured by the curvature ratio evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).
This motivates the fundamental definition.

Definition 2 (Risk aversion coefficients) The coefficient of absolute risk aversion is
\[
\gamma_u(x)
:=
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}.
\]
For \(x>0\), the corresponding coefficient of relative risk aversion is
\[
\rho_u(x)
:=
x\,\gamma_u(x).
\]

The coefficient is classically associated with the work of Arrow and Pratt (1964).
Because \(u\) is concave and increasing, \(\gamma_u(x)\geq0\). More importantly, \(\gamma_u\) is unchanged when \(u\) is replaced by \(\alpha u+\beta\) with \(\alpha>0\): it therefore depends on preferences, not on the arbitrary choice of a utility representation.
With this notation, Proposition 2 becomes
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
-
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
\pi_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
The leading-order cost of a small risk is therefore the product of a risk term, its variance, and a preference term, the coefficient of absolute risk aversion evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).



A particularly tractable case is constant absolute risk aversion (CARA).

Proposition 3 (Characterisation of CARA utility) Suppose \(u'>0\) and
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\gamma
\]
for every \(x\) in an interval, where \(\gamma\geq0\) is constant. Then:

if \(\gamma=0\), \(u\) is affine and the agent is risk-neutral;
if \(\gamma>0\), then, up to a positive affine transformation,

\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}.
\]
Conversely, \(u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}\) has constant absolute risk aversion equal to \(\gamma\).


Proof. The equation \(\gamma_u(x)=\gamma\) is
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\gamma,
\]
or equivalently
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\gamma.
\]
Hence
\[
u'(x)
=
C e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad C>0.
\]
If \(\gamma>0\), integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A-B e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad B>0,
\]
which is equivalent under a positive affine transformation to \(-e^{-\gamma x}\). If \(\gamma=0\), then \(u'\) is constant and \(u\) is affine.

CARA is a strong assumption for individuals because willingness to bear a fixed monetary risk does not depend on wealth. It is nevertheless extremely convenient. In particular, for
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad \gamma>0,
\]
we have
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
-\frac1\gamma
\log\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma X}],
\]
whenever the expectation is finite, and
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X+c)
=
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)+c.
\]
This translation invariance is one reason CARA specifications are common in models of firms or delegated decision-makers when one wants to analyse profit risk without modelling wealth effects explicitly.
For Gaussian risks the small-risk approximation is not an approximation at all.

Proposition 4 (CARA utility and Gaussian wealth) Let
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad \gamma>0,
\]
and let
\[
X=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\varepsilon^2.
\]

The calculation uses the Laplace transform of a standard Gaussian, or equivalently its moment-generating function:
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]

Proof. Since
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2},
\]
we obtain
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
-e^{-\gamma\mu}
\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma\varepsilon Z}]
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\varepsilon^2
\right).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
-e^{-\gamma\operatorname{ce}_u(X)}
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\varepsilon^2
\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\varepsilon^2.
\]
Since \(\gamma_u\equiv\gamma\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\varepsilon^2\), the above second-order formula is exact in this Gaussian/CARA case.







NoteTwo proofs of the Gaussian Laplace transform





Let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and define
\[
M(t)
=
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}].
\]
We show that
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]
1. Completing the square. Using the Gaussian density,
\[
M(t)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
\exp\!\left(
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,dz.
\]
Since
\[
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
=
-\frac{(z-t)^2}{2}
+
\frac{t^2}{2},
\]
we obtain
\[
M(t)
=
e^{t^2/2}
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
e^{-(z-t)^2/2}\,dz
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]
2. A differential equation. Differentiating under the expectation,
\[
M'(t)
=
\mathbb E[Ze^{tZ}].
\]
Gaussian integration by parts gives
\[
\mathbb E[Zf(Z)]
=
\mathbb E[f'(Z)].
\]
With \(f(z)=e^{tz}\),
\[
M'(t)
=
tM(t).
\]
Together with \(M(0)=1\), this differential equation has the unique solution
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]






Absolute risk aversion need not be constant. We say that utility has

DARA (decreasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u'(x)<0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\);
IARA (increasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u'(x)>0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\).

For individual decision-making, DARA is often regarded as more plausible than CARA: as wealth increases, a fixed monetary gamble becomes less important relative to the agent’s resources. Some empirical work finds absolute risk aversion decreasing with wealth, but the evidence is not uniform and estimated risk attitudes vary substantially across people and elicitation methods. DARA is therefore best viewed as an economically useful benchmark rather than as a universal empirical law; see, for example, Guiso and Paiella (2008) and the rather different insurance-choice evidence in Cohen and Einav (2007).
A second classical family imposes constant relative rather than absolute risk aversion.

Proposition 5 (Characterisation of CRRA utility) Let the domain be \((0,\infty)\) and suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\qquad
\rho>0.
\]
Then, up to a positive affine transformation,
\[
u(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho},
& \rho\neq1,\\[1.1ex]
\log x,
& \rho=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Conversely, these utility functions satisfy
\[
\rho_u(x)
=
x\gamma_u(x)
=
\rho,
\]
and therefore have constant relative risk aversion.


Proof. The equation
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
gives
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\]
hence
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\frac{\rho}{x}.
\]
Integrating,
\[
u'(x)
=
C x^{-\rho},
\qquad C>0.
\]
A second integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\frac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}
\]
when \(\rho\neq1\), and
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\log x
\]
when \(\rho=1\), with \(B>0\). Positive affine transformations remove the irrelevant constants.

CRRA utility is DARA because
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
decreases with wealth. It also imposes a very specific rate of decline: doubling wealth halves absolute risk aversion. This restriction is often too rigid empirically. The logarithmic case \(\rho=1\) is the specification associated with Daniel Bernoulli’s classical discussion of the St Petersburg paradox.



People can often answer questions about certainty equivalents – what sure amount would make you indifferent to this lottery? – much more readily than they can specify or draw an entire utility function. It is therefore useful to have a way of comparing the risk aversion of two agents without assigning cardinal meaning to the vertical scales of their utility functions.
Consider one agent represented by utility \(u\) and another represented by utility \(v\). The key mathematical idea is concavification: one agent is more risk-averse than the other precisely when their utility can be obtained from the other’s by applying an additional increasing concave transformation.

Proposition 6 (Comparison of risk aversion) Let \(u\) and \(v\) be twice continuously differentiable, strictly increasing utility functions on the same interval \(\mathcal I\). Then the following statements are equivalent:

for every \(x\in\mathcal I\),
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x);
\]
there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) on \(v(\mathcal I)\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]


In words, the agent represented by \(u\) is more risk-averse than the agent represented by \(v\) exactly when \(u\) is an increasing concave transformation of \(v\).

Proof. Because \(v\) is strictly increasing, it is invertible on its range. Define
\[
g
:=
u\circ v^{-1}.
\]
Then \(u=g\circ v\), and \(g\) is increasing because both \(u\) and \(v^{-1}\) are increasing. Differentiating the identity
\[
g(v(x))
=
u(x)
\]
gives
\[
g'(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{v'(x)}
>
0.
\]
Differentiating once more,
\[
g''(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\left(
\gamma_v(x)-\gamma_u(x)
\right).
\]
The factor
\[
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\]
is positive. Hence
\[
g''\leq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gamma_u\geq\gamma_v.
\]
This proves both directions.

The comparison has an immediate implication for certainty equivalents.

Proposition 7 (Ordering of certainty equivalents) Suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x)
\]
for every \(x\in\mathcal I\). Then, for every random variable \(X\) for which the certainty equivalents are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]

Thus, when the agent represented by \(u\) is more risk-averse than the agent represented by \(v\), they assign a lower certainty equivalent to every risky prospect.

Proof. By Proposition 6, there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
\mathbb E[g(v(X))]
\leq
g\bigl(\mathbb E[v(X)]\bigr).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent under \(v\),
\[
\mathbb E[v(X)]
=
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
g\!\left(
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr)
\right)
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
But
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]
